newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Young women, cheap labels hike Japan wine demand.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Young women, cheap labels hike Japan wine demand.

text.p: Until a few years ago, wine rarely touched the lips of Japanese consumers, who traditionally chose beer, sake or whisky as their favourite quaff.
But an increase in cheap, domestic labels and a growing taste for wine among young women means the tipple is gaining a growing following in Japan.

"In the past, people judged wines according to the price -- the more expensive the better -- and it was only drunk on special occasions," said Fumitaka Ohtani, wine division director at Mercian Corp, a major winemaker and distributor.
"Now, consumers are beginning to realise good wines don't necessarily cost an arm and a leg," he said.
According to Mercian, which owns vineyards in Napa Valley and Bordeaux, Japanese on average drink only about 1.2 litres of wine per year, or about 1/62 of the French average.

Japan's demand has, however, been rising steadily by about 15 percent a year and it will only be a matter of time before consumption matches the 6.7 litres consumed by the average American, Ohtani said.
Liquor firms are doing their best to help fill glasses, providing an array of half-sized bottles and fitting them with screw-on caps, for consumers who don't have cork screws.

As a result, domestic wine shipments rose 14 percent to 47,303 kilolitres (kl) in the first eight months of 1996, government statistics show. Total shipments rose seven percent to 99,715 kl, compared with the same period last year.
"A full bottle of domestically blended wine or Chilean or South African wine can now be bought for under 1,000 yen ($9), which is a competitive level to beer," Ohtani said.
NON-EUROPEAN WINE IMPORTS SURGING.

The data also showed non-European wine imports surging, with Chilean wines up nearly 400 percent in the January-October period of 1996. South African wine imports quadrupled and Australian wines doubled from the previous year.
But wine-tasting school officials and sommeliers say that despite the rage for inexpensive wines, people who want to sniff the cork before trying full-bodied reds are also on the rise.
Sommeliers are wine experts who buy and look after wines at restaurants and advise diners on what types of wine go best with a meal.
Wine bars are springing up on fashionable street corners of Tokyo and a flood of magazines and books with discourses on Chateaux and good and bad years line bookstore shelves.

"Japanese, especially young women, are enthusiastic travellers and more and more are coming in contact with European cuisine and the wines that come with it," said Shinji Saito, owner and instructor of Evi Wine School, the newest of the estimated 10 wine schools in Tokyo.

Each class starts with a one-hour lecture on grapes, wine-making methods and geography. It is followed by another hour of sniffing, tasting and commenting on six different types of wine. The 185 students, of which 80 percent are single women in their late 20s and early 30s, also have the option of visiting Chateaux in France as well as Japanese wineries.
"Many Japanese now know from experience either abroad or from eating at French or Italian reaturants that wines of quality are delicious," he added. "They are eager to learn more about them."
JUMP IN APPLICANTS FOR SOMMELIER EXAMS

The increasing popularity of wines, both bargain-priced and expensive, has also boosted the number of applicants for the sommelier exam, Japan Sommelier Association (JSA) director Hideyoshi Sato said. In 1996, applicants totalled 1,231 compared with a mere 141 in 1985.
Sato doesn't think the recent "wine boom" will end soon, as many fads tend to do.
"The Japanese have a wide range of choices now, from 500 yen ($4.50) bottles to costly vintage wines and they are beginning to realise that they like wines," he said.
"After all these years, wine is finally becoming a part of daily Japanese life," he added. ($1=113 yen)
